purpose: Reason about what each ingredient contributes (water, fat, sugar, protein, solids), how substitutions preserve or break those roles, and how acid-leavening and structure chemistry determine bake outcomes.
assumptions: no laboratory assays on hand; use label protein %, sensory freshness, and heuristic baker % bands
home-kitchen or small-batch craft scale unless stated
wheat flour is default gluten source unless gluten-free path is explicit
exclusions: clinical nutrition therapy and medical diets
alcoholic fermentation beyond culinary yeast dough flavor

competency_questions.question: What water, protein, fat, and sugar contributions does each major ingredient make to this formula?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answer lists each major ingredient with at least water and one structure-relevant solid contribution

competency_questions.question: How does available water control starch gelatinization and final crumb set?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: explains free water need for gelatinization and names a sugar/fat delay effect

competency_questions.question: Which flour protein class and salt level support the intended gluten structure?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: names flour class/protein band and salt baker % rationale

competency_questions.question: What sets the crumb gel: starch, egg protein, hydrocolloids, or a combination?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: identifies primary set mechanism for the product class

competency_questions.question: How does fat physical state (solid plastic vs oil) change method and crumb?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: links fat state to creaming vs muffin method and expected tenderness/spread

competency_questions.question: How do sugar type and dose affect tenderness, browning, and shelf moisture?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: distinguishes sucrose vs invert effects and browning vs set tradeoff

competency_questions.question: When substituting an ingredient, which functional axes must be rebalanced?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: lists water/fat/sugar/protein/leavening axes affected and conversion approach

competency_questions.question: How do you rebuild structure when eggs are removed from a cake or cookie?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: inventories egg functions then assigns substitutes per function with trial criterion

competency_questions.question: How should acid ingredients and cocoa type determine chemical leavener choice?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: pairs natural vs Dutch cocoa and cultured acids with soda vs powder correctly

competency_questions.question: When is yeast preferable to chemical leavening, and what does yeast require to retain gas?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states product-class rule and gluten/gas-retention requirement

competency_questions.question: Why can crust color mislead doneness, and what chemistry drives browning?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: separates Maillard/caramel drivers from internal set criteria

competency_questions.question: How do you convert between cocoa powder and chocolate or between dairy and plant milk without breaking the formula?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: recloses fat, sugar, water, and dry mass budgets after the swap

glossary.definition: Ingredient mass as a percentage of total flour mass (flour = 100%)
Partial vapor pressure of water in the product relative to pure water; drives microbial risk and texture
Elastic-extensible protein network from hydrated wheat gliadin and glutenin under mechanical development
Heat- and water-driven swelling and pasting of starch granules that sets crumb on cooling
Fat action that interrupts gluten strands to tenderize crumb; also the plastic fat ingredient class
Baking powder releasing some CO2 on hydration and more on heating
Non-enzymatic browning between reducing sugars and amino compounds producing color and roasted flavor
Alkalized cocoa with higher pH, darker color, milder acidity; pairs with baking powder not soda alone
Dispersion of fat in water (or reverse) stabilized by emulsifiers such as lecithin
Water-binding polymer (gum, starch, gel former) used to build viscosity or gel when gluten or egg is limited

nodes.definition: Characterize free vs bound water in a formula: water hydrates flour proteins and starch, sets water activity (Aw), dilutes solutes, and is the continuous phase for emulsions and batters. Removing or reducing water without compensation collapses gluten development, starch gelatinization window, and heat transfer during bake.

base.update_signal: measured Aw or final crumb moisture diverges from target band after a process change

included: hydration contribution of liquids and high-moisture ingredients
Aw effects on texture and shelf life

pros.claim: Water is the primary solvent and hydration driver; formula water must be accounted as baker % of flour
pros.example: 80% hydration in a lean dough yields open crumb when gluten is developed

cons.claim: Water alone does not guarantee structure; excess free water without protein/starch sinks centers
cons.example: a 100% hydration batter with low protein flour puddles and collapses

failure_modes: omitting water from wet ingredients (eggs, milk) double-counts solids
treating oil as water for hydration
acceptance_tests: every liquid ingredient lists estimated water fraction and total formula water as % of flour
revisit_triggers: a substitution changes moisture of a major wet ingredient
crumb feels wet or dry after cool

nodes.definition: Map flour protein content and quality to gluten-forming potential: high-protein bread flour (~12-14%) builds elastic networks; cake flour (~7-9%) limits gluten for tender crumb; whole-grain and high-ash flours dilute gluten with bran. Protein % is a prior, not a guarantee of strength under acid, fat, or sugar load.

base.update_signal: flour lot protein or farinograph absorption changes, or brand is switched

pros.claim: Matching flour protein class to product class is the first structural control lever
pros.example: bread flour for baguettes; soft cake flour for chiffon

cons.claim: Protein % on the bag does not capture damaged starch or enzyme activity that also drive water demand
cons.example: two 12% flours can differ in absorption by several points

failure_modes: using AP flour for high-hydration artisan bread without extra mix development
assuming cake flour cannot hold any structure in high-sugar formulas
acceptance_tests: flour class and protein band stated for every formula; substitution notes if AP is forced
revisit_triggers: flour brand or milling lot changes absorption

nodes.definition: Starch gelatinizes as temperature and available water rise: granules swell, leach amylose, and set the crumb gel on cool-down. Gelatinization temperature rises with sugar and fat (delayed set); low water leaves ungelatinized starch and a dry, pasty crumb. Egg and dairy proteins co-set with starch to lock structure.

base.update_signal: DSC or bake trial shows set temperature shifted by sugar/fat reformulation

pros.claim: Starch set is the primary irreversible structural lock in cakes and quick breads
pros.example: a layer cake is safe to unmold only after starch/protein gel has cooled enough to hold

cons.claim: High sugar delays gelatinization so underbaked centers look wet even when exterior browns
cons.example: a high-ratio cake needs longer bake or lower oven to finish the center

failure_modes: pulling product when color is done but center starch is unset
assuming all flours gelatinize at the same temperature
acceptance_tests: center internal temperature and cool-set criteria defined for the product class
revisit_triggers: sugar or fat budget changes more than ~5 baker % points

nodes.definition: Fat shortens gluten strands (tender crumb), lubricates mouthfeel, carries fat-soluble aroma, and aerates when creamed with sugar (trapped air cells). Solid plastic fats (butter, shortening) cream and laminate; liquid oils lubricate but do not cream. Replacing solid fat with oil changes structure, not just calories.

base.update_signal: fat type swapped (butter vs oil vs shortening) or melt profile of the fat changes

included: shortening vs lubrication vs creaming aeration
smoke point only as cooking constraint
excluded: baker % algebra alone without fat phase state

pros.claim: Matching fat physical state to method (cream solid fat; oil for muffin method) preserves intended crumb
pros.example: creaming butter+sugar for pound cake traps air that chemical leavening expands

cons.claim: Oil substitution for butter often needs egg or starch compensation for lost structure
cons.example: 1:1 oil for butter in cookies spreads more and sets thinner

failure_modes: using melted butter when recipe expects plastic creamed fat
assuming all fats are interchangeable by weight alone
acceptance_tests: fat type, state at mix, and baker % of flour are recorded with method match
revisit_triggers: spread or tenderness shifts after a fat swap

nodes.definition: Sugar competes for water (hygroscopic), tenderizes by interfering with gluten and starch set, feeds Maillard and caramelization browning, and lowers Aw for shelf life. Invert sugars and honey retain more moisture than sucrose; reducing sugar in a formula without adjusting water and fat dries and toughens the product.

base.update_signal: sugar type or invert fraction changes; product stales or browns off-target

pros.claim: Sugar is both bulk solid and water competitor; baker % sugar bands define product class (lean bread vs high-ratio cake)
pros.example: ~100% sugar on flour is high-ratio cake territory needing emulsified shortenings

cons.claim: Cutting sugar for health without rebuilding water and fat often yields tough, pale, dry crumb
cons.example: a 30% sugar cut in cookies without compensatory fat/liquid fails spread and tenderness

failure_modes: treating brown sugar as pure sucrose without molasses moisture
ignoring hygroscopic pull when freezing products
acceptance_tests: sugar type and baker % stated; moisture contribution of liquid sweeteners listed
revisit_triggers: browning rate or shelf moisture shifts

nodes.definition: Whole egg contributes water (~75%), protein that coagulates ~63-70 C, lecithin emulsifier (yolk), and foam-forming albumen. Eggs set custards and cakes, emulsify fat into batters, and trap air when whipped. Removing eggs removes structure, emulsification, and moisture simultaneously — each function must be replaced separately for egg-free work.

base.update_signal: egg size standard changes or egg-free reformulation request arrives

pros.claim: Decomposing egg into water+protein+fat+lecithin enables targeted substitutions
pros.example: egg-free cake uses aquafaba foam + oil + starch gel instead of one paste

cons.claim: overheating past the coagulation band curdles custards and weeps water; no single replacer covers foam+emulsify+coagulate+moisture at once
cons.example: pastry cream scrambled at a hard boil; flax gel binds muffins but does not foam a genoise

failure_modes: removing eggs and only adding water so structure and emulsification both vanish
overbaking after an egg increase without adjusting set temperature so custard weeps
using one commercial egg paste as if it replaced foam and coagulation equally
acceptance_tests: egg mass and functional roles documented for the formula
egg-free path lists separate agents for structure, emulsify, foam, and moisture if any are required
revisit_triggers: allergen or vegan constraint changes egg availability
coagulation failure (curdle/weep) observed in bake trial

nodes.definition: Salt tightens gluten (ionic strength), slows yeast, and amplifies flavor. Typical baker % is 1.8-2.2% of flour for bread; much lower in sweet doughs still matters for structure. Omitting salt yields slack dough and bland flavor; excess inhibits fermentation and tastes harsh.

base.update_signal: salt type (kosher vs table density) or low-sodium reformulation request

excluded: medical sodium diets as clinical advice

pros.claim: Consistent salt % stabilizes dough rheology across batches
pros.example: 2% salt on flour keeps baguette dough extensible yet strong

cons.claim: Volume measuring salt is unreliable across crystal sizes
cons.example: 1 tsp table salt ≠ 1 tsp kosher by mass

failure_modes: forgetting salt until after long autolyse without plan to incorporate
doubling salt when scaling volumetric recipes
acceptance_tests: salt is weighed; baker % in band for product class
revisit_triggers: dough feels slack or fermentation stalls

nodes.definition: Acids (buttermilk, yogurt, vinegar, citrus, cream of tartar, cocoa natural) lower pH, tenderize gluten, activate baking soda, and shift flavor and browning. Alkaline cocoa (Dutch) raises pH and needs baking powder rather than soda alone. pH is a control variable for leavening stoichiometry and color.

base.update_signal: acid ingredient brand acidity changes or cocoa type (natural vs Dutch) is swapped

included: common culinary acids and relative strength
pH effect on gluten and color

pros.claim: Matching acid load to chemical leavening prevents soapy residual soda or flat product
pros.example: buttermilk + soda in Irish soda bread is stoichiometric when ratios are right

cons.claim: variable cultured-dairy acidity and unlabeled cocoa process type make fixed soda doses unreliable; wrong pH shifts color and residual alkali risk
cons.example: one buttermilk brand under-acidifies a soda bread; Dutch cocoa in a soda-only cake stays dense and soapy

failure_modes: using Dutch cocoa with a soda-only formula expecting rise
adding acid late after soda already reacted in the bowl so gas is lost before the oven
ignoring cocoa process type when swapping brands mid-formula
acceptance_tests: acid sources listed with intended leavening or tenderizing role
Dutch vs natural cocoa paired with correct leavening family
revisit_triggers: off-taste or color shift after reformulation

nodes.definition: Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) needs acid + moisture + heat to release CO2; baking powder is soda + acids with controlled release (single or double acting). Dose by baker % of flour and by acid balance: excess soda leaves soapy/yellow alkaline crumb; excess acid without base leaves metallic tang and weak rise. Reaction starts on wet mix — delay bake and gas is lost.

base.update_signal: leavener age (spent powder) or altitude/pressure bake context changes dose needs

excluded: steam-only laminated pastry theory beyond chemical contribution

pros.claim: Correct leavener family and dose convert formula acids into controlled gas without residual alkali
pros.example: double-acting powder gives bench tolerance then oven spring in muffins

cons.claim: excess soda with insufficient formula acid leaves soapy alkaline off-taste and yellow crumb; excess acid without base gives sour tang and weak rise
cons.example: doubling soda in a low-acid Dutch-cocoa cake tastes soapy; vinegar overload without matching base flattens muffins

failure_modes: using only soda in a low-acid chocolate cake with Dutch cocoa
holding mixed batter hours before bake so double-acting powder spends early gas
scaling powder by volume from a spent tin that fails a hot-water fizz check
acceptance_tests: leavener type and mass recorded with acid partners
hold-time limit from mix to oven stated for the method
revisit_triggers: product tastes alkaline or fails to rise

nodes.definition: Baker's yeast ferments sugars to CO2 and ethanol, developing flavor acids and extensibility over time. Gas retention requires a continuous gluten network. Temperature, salt, sugar, and preferment design control rate. Instant, active dry, and fresh yeast differ in water needs and lag but convert by mass factors.

base.update_signal: yeast strain/format change or dough temperature control process changes

excluded: wild yeast capture protocols as primary path

pros.claim: Time-temperature-salt control yields reproducible fermentation and flavor
pros.example: bulk ferment to 30% rise at 24 C with 2% salt is more stable than fixed clock time alone

cons.claim: High sugar and fat (enriched doughs) slow yeast; under-yeast or cold dough stalls
cons.example: brioche needs more yeast or longer time than lean baguette

failure_modes: killing yeast with too-hot liquid
expecting oven spring without prior gas production and retention
acceptance_tests: yeast type, mass, target dough temp, and ferment endpoint (volume/feel) stated

nodes.definition: Batters and doughs are multi-phase: fat dispersed in water (or reverse) stabilized by egg yolk lecithin, milk proteins, mono/diglycerides in commercial shortenings, or mustard/soy lecithin. Broken emulsions (curdled batter, greasy mouthfeel) lose volume and bake unevenly. Temperature and shear during mix determine stability.

base.update_signal: emulsifier system changes (egg-free, different shortening) or mix shear profile changes

pros.claim: Stable emulsion distributes fat finely for even crumb and volume
pros.example: properly emulsified mayonnaise-style cake batter holds air and bakes fine-grained

cons.claim: Over-shearing warm butter batters can break emulsion and grease out
cons.example: pound cake batter splits when butter is too warm and eggs added too fast

failure_modes: adding all liquid at once to creamed fat
baking a visibly split batter without recovery attempt
acceptance_tests: mix method and temperature band aim to keep emulsion intact; recovery step if split
revisit_triggers: batter greases out in bowl or pan

nodes.definition: Maillard browning needs reducing sugars + amino groups + heat at moderate moisture; caramelization is sugar pyrolysis at higher temperature. pH, sugar type, and protein availability modulate color and flavor. Under-browned products can still be set; over-browned exteriors can hide wet centers — color is not doneness alone.

base.update_signal: sugar profile or oven humidity changes browning rate relative to set

included: color as signal not sole doneness

pros.claim: Understanding browning drivers lets you darken crust without overbaking interior (milk wash, higher sugar, drier surface)
pros.example: egg wash + residual heat deepens baguette color after internal temp is done

cons.claim: High-sugar formulas brown before centers set; color-chasing burns exteriors
cons.example: cookies darken at edges while centers are still doughy if oven is too hot

failure_modes: using color alone as doneness for high-sugar cakes
alkaline environments causing excessive browning and off-flavor
acceptance_tests: browning expectations separated from internal set criteria
revisit_triggers: oven steam or sugar type changes color curve

nodes.definition: Milk powders, egg wash proteins, and free amino acids accelerate surface Maillard. Dairy solids (lactose + casein/whey) brown more than water washes. This node isolates protein-side contribution to crust color and flavor distinct from bulk sugar load.

base.update_signal: milk powder brand or wash composition changes

pros.claim: A thin protein-sugar wash gives controlled shine and color without reformulating the dough
pros.example: 1:1 egg+milk wash on enriched buns browns evenly

cons.claim: Thick washes can peel or blister if applied to cold dry surfaces incorrectly
cons.example: egg wash on frozen pastry may flake

failure_modes: skipping wash then overbaking to force color
applying wash so heavy it runs and fries on the pan
acceptance_tests: wash composition recorded when color is a quality attribute
revisit_triggers: crust color off-target with correct internal temp

nodes.definition: Build substitution tables that preserve functional roles: map each substitute to water, fat, sugar, protein, and leavening impact with conversion factors (e.g., oil ≈ 0.8× butter by weight for fat with water loss adjustment; buttermilk ≈ milk + acid). Equivalence is role-based, never brand-name identity.

base.update_signal: new substitute ingredient with different solids or water fraction enters the pantry

pros.claim: Role decomposition prevents single-axis swaps that break structure
pros.example: replacing butter with oil also drops water ~15% and milk solids — add liquid if crumb dries

cons.claim: Published cup-for-cup gluten-free blends hide starch/hydrocolloid differences across brands
cons.example: Brand A 1:1 flour may need more xanthan than Brand B

failure_modes: 1:1 volume swaps without mass and function check
chaining multiple substitutions without reclosing budgets
acceptance_tests: substitution notes cite functional axes not just ingredient names
chained swaps trigger full budget reclose checklist
revisit_triggers: failure after substitution in bake trial

nodes.definition: When eggs are removed, rebuild: (1) moisture with water/plant milk, (2) coagulation/gel with starch, flax/chia gel, or commercial egg replacer, (3) emulsification with lecithin or aquafaba/oil systems, (4) foam with aquafaba or chemical leavening boost. Document which functions the original eggs performed in that formula — foam cake needs different rebuild than cookies.

base.update_signal: new egg-replacer product performance data or allergen constraint change

included: product-class-specific rebuild (foam vs binder vs custard)

pros.claim: Function-split rebuild succeeds where single paste substitutes fail
pros.example: vegan genoise uses aquafaba foam + starch set instead of whole-egg foam alone

cons.claim: Some custards and angel food structures have no home-kitchen peer without eggs
cons.example: pastry cream egg-free is a different product class

failure_modes: one-ingredient egg swap for a chiffon
boosting oil only and expecting foam volume
acceptance_tests: egg functions inventory completed before substitutes chosen
trial bake meets volume and set criteria for product class
revisit_triggers: user rejects texture of first rebuild

nodes.definition: Milk and cream contribute water, lactose, milk fat, and proteins. Cultured dairy adds acid. Nonfat dry milk boosts browning and protein without water. Substituting water for milk loses flavor, browning, and tenderness; substituting plant milks changes protein and emulsification — treat as new ingredient, not identical liquid. Lactose-free milk is nearly structure-equivalent to regular milk (same water/protein/fat bands) but often browns faster because hydrolysis yields free glucose and galactose, which accelerate Maillard.

base.update_signal: plant-milk brand protein/fat profile changes or dairy-free request

included: whole vs low-fat vs cream water/fat split

pros.claim: Accounting dairy as water+fat+solids prevents double-counting and supports dairy-free redesign
pros.example: heavy cream in ganache is ~40% fat + water — cocoa ratio depends on both

cons.claim: Barista oat milk and cheap oat milk differ in oil and stabilizer content
cons.example: a cookie formula may spread differently across plant milks

failure_modes: replacing milk with water and expecting same browning
assuming lactose-free milk changes structure (it usually does not)
acceptance_tests: dairy type and estimated fat/water listed; plant-milk swaps retested

nodes.definition: Natural cocoa is acidic and pairs with soda; Dutch-process is alkalized, darker, milder, and needs baking powder. Cocoa is dry solid + starch-like and bitter; chocolate is cocoa mass + cocoa butter + sugar. Swapping cocoa powder for melted chocolate requires removing fat and sugar elsewhere and adding dry mass.

base.update_signal: cocoa brand natural/Dutch labeling error or chocolate couverture % cocoa butter changes

included: cocoa powder vs chocolate conversion axes

pros.claim: Correct cocoa type + leavener pairing fixes both rise and color
pros.example: natural cocoa + soda gives mahogany crumb and clean rise in devil's food

cons.claim: unlabeled cocoa may be natural or Dutch; swapping cocoa powder for chocolate without reclosing fat and sugar breaks rise and texture
cons.example: Dutch cocoa + soda-only heirloom recipe; equal-weight bar chocolate for cocoa without cutting other fat/sugar

failure_modes: 1:1 chocolate for cocoa without fat/sugar budget adjust
bloomed chocolate treated as equivalent to dry cocoa powder solids
natural/Dutch label ignored when changing brands
acceptance_tests: cocoa process type and leavener family are consistent
chocolate↔cocoa swaps reclose fat and sugar budgets
revisit_triggers: color or rise failure in chocolate formulas

nodes.definition: Gums (xanthan, guar), starches (cornstarch, tapioca, potato), and gels (flax, chia, pectin) bind water and build viscosity or gel strength when gluten or egg is reduced. Dose is small and nonlinear: excess xanthan yields gummy crumb. Pair with correct hydration and shear. Xanthan dose bands: ~0.3–0.6% of flour for cakes and batters; gluten-free sandwich bread often needs ~1–2% of flour at the high end with matching hydration so crumb slices without crumbling or turning gummy.

base.update_signal: gum brand mesh size or starch gelatinization profile changes

included: common culinary hydrocolloids and dose bands
gummy vs weak gel failure modes

pros.claim: Low-dose xanthan restores gas retention in gluten-free batters when dosed by product class
pros.example: cake batter ~0.5% flour; GF sandwich bread ~1–2% flour with higher hydration holds slices without crumbling

cons.claim: Hydrocolloids cannot recreate wheat extensibility fully; expectations must match product class
cons.example: GF flaky laminated pastry remains hard even with gums

failure_modes: tablespoon-scale gum dosing
adding gum without increasing water for its binding
acceptance_tests: hydrocolloid identity, % of flour, and hydration note recorded

nodes.definition: Flour amylases and damaged starch increase water absorption and sugar availability for yeast and browning. Excess enzyme (sprouted flour, long warm ferments) can over-degrade starch into sticky dough. Malt additions boost fermentation and color deliberately.

base.update_signal: flour Falling Number or malt addition policy changes

included: amylase effects on stickiness and fermentation
excluded: lab Falling Number assay procedure detail

pros.claim: Knowing enzyme activity explains sticky dough that is not merely over-hydrated
pros.example: low Falling Number flour needs cooler ferment and less time

cons.claim: Home bakers rarely know Falling Number; brand heuristics and feel must substitute
cons.example: a new mill lot may behave differently without label change

failure_modes: adding diastatic malt to already enzyme-active whole grain recklessly
misdiagnosing enzyme stickiness as need for more flour
acceptance_tests: sticky-dough differential diagnosis includes enzyme path vs true excess water

nodes.definition: Unsaturated fats oxidize with heat, light, and metal ions producing off-flavors. Whole-grain flours and nut flours go rancid faster. Freshness of oils and nut meals is a formulation constraint equal to chemistry ratios — rancid fat ruins otherwise correct formulas.

base.update_signal: oil storage practice changes or nut flour age unknown

included: storage guidance for oils and whole-grain flours

pros.claim: Sensory check of oils and nut flours prevents wasted bakes
pros.example: smell walnut meal before costly torte batter

cons.claim: Mild rancidity can be masked by sugar and chocolate until after bake
cons.example: consumer detects cardboard note next day

failure_modes: using old open flax oil in egg-free gel
storing whole wheat in warm pantry for months
acceptance_tests: high-risk fats get freshness check before mix

nodes.definition: Sucrose crystallization yields grainy fudge, sandy cookies, or seizing ganache; invert sugar and glucose syrup interfere with crystal growth. In frozen desserts, small ice crystals need fat, stabilizers, and rapid freeze. Crystal control is texture engineering, not decoration.

base.update_signal: sweetener blend changes crystal behavior or freeze-thaw cycle increases

included: interfering agents for candy and frostings

pros.claim: Invert or corn syrup fraction prevents grainy fudge and icings
pros.example: 10-20% glucose syrup in fondant keeps it smooth

cons.claim: Too much invert makes products that never set firm enough to cut
cons.example: soft-ball candy stays sticky in humid kitchens

failure_modes: stirring crystallizing sugar at wrong stage
refreezing ice cream repeatedly
acceptance_tests: products needing smooth texture list crystal-control agent or method

nodes.definition: Aroma compounds partition into fat or water phases; alcohol extracts behave differently than oils. Fat carries and rounds flavor; water-phase acids taste sharper. Reducing fat without adjusting flavor dose can thin taste; vanilla in oil-based doughs blooms differently than in custards. Formulation of taste follows phase chemistry.

base.update_signal: fat reduction request or extract vs paste form change

pros.claim: Matching flavor form to matrix improves perceived intensity without waste
pros.example: vanilla bean paste in ice cream base out-performs alcohol extract flash-off

cons.claim: Overdosing extracts in low-fat formulas tastes harsh and alcoholic
cons.example: nonfat pudding with double vanilla extract burns nose

failure_modes: scaling extracts linearly with sugar-only reductions
adding oil-soluble spice to water icing without carrier
acceptance_tests: flavor form and phase match noted for low-fat or non-dairy reformulations

edges.why_related: starch gelatinization requires available free water
egg water contribution is part of total formula water
chemical leaveners need moisture to dissolve and react
yeast metabolism and dough hydration depend on free water
continuous water phase defines oil-in-water batter emulsions
flour supplies the starch that gelatinizes into crumb gel
salt acts on gluten proteins from flour
gas retention requires flour gluten network
fat shortens gluten derived from flour protein
enzyme activity is a flour property modulating starch and sugar
egg proteins co-set with starch gel for structure
hydrocolloids and starches jointly manage water and gel strength
dispersed fat phase is what emulsions stabilize
fat swaps are a primary substitution axis
oxidation risk tracks fat type and unsaturation
fat phase partitions and carries aroma compounds
sugar and acid jointly affect browning and tenderness
reducing sugars fuel Maillard browning
sugar load affects batter viscosity and gas retention
crystal control is a sugar-system design problem
sweetener swaps change water competition and browning
yolk lecithin is the primary culinary emulsifier
egg-free protocol starts from egg function inventory
egg wash proteins drive surface browning
soda requires formula acids for CO2 release
cocoa process type sets acid load for leavening choice
chemical leavening often compensates lost egg foam
egg-free rebuild uses the general equivalence map
dairy and plant-milk swaps use role-based equivalence
dairy solids supply surface browning proteins and lactose
gums and gels replace egg binding and some structure
pH modulates Maillard rate and color
surface proteins accelerate crust browning
rancid fat invalidates otherwise correct fat function design
chemical vs biological leavening compete for process time and flavor goals
edges.resolution_rule: choose primary leavening by product class: quick breads chemical; artisan bread yeast; hybrid only with explicit dual design

conflict_axes.name: tenderness_vs_structure
conflict_axes.description: Fat and sugar tenderize; protein networks and set gels hold shape
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: set product-class structure minimum first, then tenderize within that band

conflict_axes.name: browning_vs_internal_set
conflict_axes.description: Surface color can finish before center gelatinizes in high-sugar formulas
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: lower temp/longer time or shield color; never use color as sole doneness

conflict_axes.name: chemical_vs_yeast_leavening
conflict_axes.description: Speed and flavor trade off between chemical gas and fermented flavor
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: product class picks primary leavener; hybrid only with explicit design

conflict_axes.name: egg_function_completeness_vs_single_swap
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: inventory functions; multi-agent rebuild for structure-critical products

conflict_axes.name: natural_vs_dutch_cocoa_path
conflict_axes.description: Acidic natural cocoa vs alkalized Dutch changes leavener and color
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: declare cocoa type first; lock leavener family to match

conflict_axes.name: hydration_vs_handling
conflict_axes.description: Higher water improves openness and gelatinization but increases slackness
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: match flour protein and mix development to hydration target

conflict_axes.name: clean_label_vs_emulsified_performance
conflict_axes.description: Commercial emulsifiers improve high-ratio cakes; home pantries may lack them
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: state performance ceiling of clean-label path honestly

conflict_axes.name: fresh_fat_flavor_vs_storage_convenience
conflict_axes.description: Nut oils and whole grains taste best fresh but spoil faster
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: cold storage for high-risk fats; sensory gate before mix

conflict_axes.name: crystal_smoothness_vs_firm_set
conflict_axes.description: Interfering sugars smooth texture but can prevent firm set
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: dose invert fraction to product need; test set at service temp

edge_cases.description: High-altitude bake with low air pressure expands gas faster and dries product
edge_cases.trigger: user reports location above ~3000 ft or chronic dry collapse
edge_cases.mitigation: slightly reduce chemical leavener, increase liquid, raise oven temp modestly; validate with trial

edge_cases.description: Egg-free chiffon or angel-style foam cake request
edge_cases.mitigation: warn performance ceiling; aquafaba foam + starch; or recommend different product class

edge_cases.description: Dutch cocoa used in a soda-only heirloom recipe
edge_cases.trigger: cocoa type Dutch with only baking soda listed
edge_cases.mitigation: switch to natural cocoa or replace soda path with baking powder and rebalance acid

edge_cases.description: Butter-to-oil swap in creamed cookie dough
edge_cases.trigger: oil substituted for plastic fat in creaming method
edge_cases.mitigation: change method toward muffin-style or chill oil dough; expect more spread; adjust flour slightly

edge_cases.trigger: leavener older than ~6-12 months or fails hot-water fizz test
edge_cases.mitigation: replace leavener; do not increase dose of dead powder
discard fat source; do not mask with extra vanilla
starch blend + xanthan dose band + higher hydration; set expectations vs wheat crumb

edge_cases.description: Buttermilk unavailable; only milk and vinegar on hand
edge_cases.mitigation: milk + acid approximation; note weaker body than true buttermilk; same soda pairing intent

edge_cases.description: Chocolate bar melted into a cocoa-powder cake
edge_cases.trigger: chocolate substituted for cocoa powder by equal weight
edge_cases.mitigation: reclose fat and sugar; reduce other fat/sugar; add dry flour/starch for lost cocoa solids
warm gently and whisk in a spoon of flour to rebind, or restart with temperature control

edge_cases.description: Long bulk ferment with enzyme-active whole wheat goes sticky
edge_cases.trigger: slack sticky dough despite moderate hydration
edge_cases.mitigation: cool dough, shorten ferment, consider non-diastatic malt only; avoid dumping excess flour blindly

workflow.description: List every ingredient with estimated water, fat, sugar, protein contributions
workflow.gate: all >5% ingredients have at least water and primary solid role

workflow.description: Choose flour protein class for product structure target
workflow.gate: flour class matches product class or deviation justified

workflow.description: Lock fat type/state and sugar type for method and tenderness
workflow.gate: fat state matches intended mix method

workflow.description: Pair acids and cocoa type with soda/powder/yeast choice and dose
workflow.gate: no soda-only with Dutch cocoa; yeast products have gas retention plan

workflow.description: State whether starch, egg, hydrocolloid, or combo sets the crumb
workflow.gate: set mechanism named for product class

workflow.description: If high fat batter, plan emulsifiers and mix temperature
workflow.gate: high-fat formulas have emulsifier source identified

workflow.description: For any constraint (allergy, vegan, pantry), map role-based swaps
workflow.gate: each swap lists functions lost and compensations

workflow.description: If eggs removed, run function inventory and multi-agent rebuild
workflow.gate: all required egg functions covered or product class changed

workflow.description: Sensory-check oils, nut flours, leavener potency
workflow.gate: no rancid fat; leavener not expired

workflow.description: Separate color targets from internal set criteria

dominance_rules.rationale: a collapsed product is failure regardless of tenderness
dominance_rules.trigger: fat or sugar increase request on already tender formula
dominance_rules.action: hold protein/set mechanism; adjust fat/sugar within band

dominance_rules.rationale: pH mismatch yields flat soapy chocolate cakes
dominance_rules.action: re-pair natural/Dutch with soda/powder before other tweaks

dominance_rules.rationale: brand paste rarely matches all roles

dominance_rules.action: extend bake or lower temp; do not pull on color alone
fix gluten development/hydration before increasing leavener

dominance_rules.trigger: flat quick bread temptation to double soda
dominance_rules.action: check acid load and powder freshness first

anti_rework_rules.prevents: sunk wet centers with dark crust

iteration_protocol.action: recheck set mechanism, sugar/fat delay, leavener dose, and oven temp/time
rebalance acid/soda; verify cocoa type; reduce residual alkali
rebuild foam/bind/emulsify agents; consider product class change
review fat state, sugar type, flour protein, and chill
reduce gum dose; adjust starch blend and hydration
add dairy solids/wash or finish heat; do not overbake interior
run SUB_EQUIV map and reclose all contribution axes

priority_rationale: Water, flour protein, fat, and sugar foundations precede structure gels, acid-leavening chemistry, and substitution rebuilds; freshness and browning signals come after functional design.
